subChunks.title: tsvector, tsquery, and GIN Indexes
subChunks.hookHtml: LIKE searches are slow and dumb. Full-text search is fast, language-aware, and returns ranked results. PostgreSQL's built-in full-text capabilities rival standalone search engines for many use cases.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem with LIKE

-- LIKE cannot use a B-tree index efficiently (leading wildcard):
WHERE description LIKE '%fireball%'  -- full scan every time

tsvector — the document

SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'Archmage Veylan casts the Fireball spell')
-- Returns: 'archmag':1 'cast':3 'fireball':5 'spell':6 'veylan':2
-- Note: stems applied ('Archmage' → 'archmag', 'casts' → 'cast')

A tsvector is a sorted list of lexemes (stemmed word forms) with position information. Stop words (the, a, and) are removed.

tsquery — the search

SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'fireball & ice');   -- both words
SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'fireball | ice');   -- either word
SELECT to_tsquery('english', '!ice');             -- not ice
SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', 'fireball ice'); -- space = AND

Matching

SELECT title
FROM   spells
WHERE  to_tsvector('english', description) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'fireball');

Indexed full-text search

-- Add a pre-computed tsvector column for performance:
ALTER TABLE spells ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', description)) STORED;

CREATE INDEX ON spells USING GIN (search_vector);

-- Now this is fast:
SELECT title FROM spells WHERE search_vector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'fireball');

Ranking results

SELECT title, ts_rank(search_vector, query) AS rank
FROM   spells, to_tsquery('english', 'fire') AS query
WHERE  search_vector @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC;

storyBeats.text: 'Find all spells containing fire, ignoring capitalisation, handling plural forms.' LIKE cannot do this in any reasonable time.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: LIKE '%fire%' scans every row and finds 'Fireball' but not 'ignite' even though both involve fire. Full-text search uses stemming — 'fires', 'fired', 'firing' all map to 'fire'. The GIN index makes it fast. ts_rank sorts by relevance. For any serious search feature, use full-text.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Full-text search design

Describe the steps to add fast full-text search for a spells(id, name, description TEXT) table in PostgreSQL. Include: what column to add, what index to create, and what query to run.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Step 1: Add a generated tsvector column:
ALTER TABLE spells ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(name, '') || ' ' || COALESCE(description, ''))) STORED;

Step 2: Create a GIN index on the tsvector column:
CREATE INDEX idx_spells_search ON spells USING GIN (search_vector);

Step 3: Query using @@:
SELECT id, name FROM spells
WHERE search_vector @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'fire damage');

Step 4 (optional): Rank by relevance:
SELECT id, name, ts_rank(search_vector, q) AS rank
FROM spells, plainto_tsquery('english', 'fire damage') q
WHERE search_vector @@ q
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 10;
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain the difference between to_tsvector and to_tsquery, and why stop words and stemming matter for search quality.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
to_tsvector converts a document (text) into a tsvector — a sorted list of lexemes with position information. It applies: stemming (casts → cast, spells → spell), stop word removal (the, and, a are discarded), and lowercase normalisation.

to_tsquery converts a search string into a tsquery — an expression of lexemes with boolean operators. 'fire AND ice' → 'fire' & 'ice'.

Stop words: removing common words ('the', 'a', 'in') reduces index size and improves relevance. A search for 'the fireball' should not return every document containing 'the'.

Stemming: maps word variants to a common root. A search for 'casting' matches documents containing 'cast', 'casts', 'casted'. Without stemming, users must guess the exact form stored in the index.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a tsvector is, how it differs from the original text, and why storing a precomputed tsvector column is better than calling to_tsvector in every query.

questions.prompt: What does to_tsvector do to a text string?
options: Converts it to a sorted list of stemmed lexemes with stop words removed — ready for full-text matching
Tokenises on spaces without any normalisation
Converts to lowercase and removes punctuation only
Creates a B-tree index on the text
questions.answer: Converts it to a sorted list of stemmed lexemes with stop words removed — ready for full-text matching
questions.explanation: to_tsvector applies stemming (word → root form), stop word removal, and position tracking. The result is a tsvector — a preprocessed document representation optimised for full-text queries.

options: Rows where the document contains words stemming to 'fire' — e.g. fire, fires, firing
Rows where ANY word matches — @@ is a LIKE alias
questions.answer: Rows where the document contains words stemming to 'fire' — e.g. fire, fires, firing
questions.explanation: The @@ operator tests whether a tsvector matches a tsquery. Both sides use stemming — the query 'fire' matches any lexeme whose stem is 'fire', so 'fires', 'firing', 'fired' all match.

questions.prompt: Why store a GENERATED ALWAYS AS tsvector column instead of computing it in every query?
options: Computing to_tsvector in every query recalculates it for every row — a pre-computed stored column is calculated once at insert/update time, and the GIN index is built on it
to_tsvector cannot be used in WHERE — it must be a column
Stored columns avoid the GIN index overhead
questions.answer: Computing to_tsvector in every query recalculates it for every row — a pre-computed stored column is calculated once at insert/update time, and the GIN index is built on it
questions.explanation: Calling to_tsvector in WHERE means recomputing the vector for every row on every query — defeating any index benefit. A STORED generated column recomputes only on INSERT/UPDATE and the GIN index is built on the stored value.

questions.prompt: When would you use PostgreSQL full-text search vs a dedicated search engine like Elasticsearch?
options: PostgreSQL FTS for moderate data with SQL-native querying; Elasticsearch for billion-scale, complex relevance tuning, faceting, or real-time indexing requirements
Elasticsearch is always better — PostgreSQL FTS is a toy
PostgreSQL FTS for all cases — Elasticsearch is redundant
Elasticsearch for updates; PostgreSQL FTS for reads
questions.answer: PostgreSQL FTS for moderate data with SQL-native querying; Elasticsearch for billion-scale, complex relevance tuning, faceting, or real-time indexing requirements
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL FTS eliminates an extra infrastructure component and handles many search use cases well. Elasticsearch excels at: extremely high write throughput with near-real-time indexing, complex relevance models, faceting/aggregation at search time, and billion+ document scales. Choose based on actual requirements.
